items.value: Statement-I is incorrect (the atmosphere is heated mainly by terrestrial long-wave radiation, not by incoming solar radiation); Statement-II is correct
items.reasoning: The atmosphere is largely transparent to incoming short-wave solar radiation, which passes through and heats the earth's surface; the surface then re-radiates energy as long-wave terrestrial radiation, which the atmosphere absorbs. So the atmosphere is heated more by terrestrial radiation than by incoming solar radiation, making Statement-I incorrect. Statement-II is correct and is in fact the reason Statement-I is wrong: carbon dioxide, water vapour and other greenhouse gases are good absorbers of long-wave radiation, which is why terrestrial radiation is the dominant heat source for the atmosphere.

items.value: Both statements are correct and the strong equatorial convection explains the greater thickness of the troposphere at the equator
items.reasoning: The troposphere is about 18 km thick at the equator and only about 8 km at the poles, so Statement-I is correct. Statement-II is also correct and is the standard explanation: intense equatorial heating drives powerful convectional currents that carry heat to great heights, pushing the tropopause upward, whereas weak polar heating produces little vertical convection. Statement-II therefore explains Statement-I.

items.value: All four — pyroclastic debris, ash and dust, nitrogen compounds and sulphur compounds are all volcanic products
items.reasoning: Volcanic eruptions eject solid material (pyroclastic debris such as bombs, lapilli and blocks, plus fine ash and dust), liquid material (lava) and gases. The gaseous fraction is dominated by water vapour and carbon dioxide but routinely includes sulphur compounds (SO2, H2S) and nitrogen compounds (N2, ammonia), along with traces of chlorine, hydrogen and argon. All four listed items are therefore products of volcanic eruptions.

items.value: Only statement 1 is a correct inference; the Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift are warm currents that make the ocean warmer, not cold currents making it colder
items.reasoning: In January the northern continents are much colder than the adjoining oceans, so isotherms bend northward (poleward, into warmer values) over the ocean and southward (equatorward) over the land — statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 misdescribes the currents twice over: the Gulf Stream and the North Atlantic Drift are WARM currents, and they make the North Atlantic Ocean warmer, not colder. It is precisely because they warm the ocean that the isotherms bend north there, so the statement's stated cause is the opposite of the truth even though its stated effect is right.

items.value: Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana
items.reasoning: West Africa supplies roughly two-thirds of the world's cocoa, with Côte d'Ivoire the largest producer by a wide margin and Ghana second. Algeria and Morocco are North African and far too dry; Botswana and Namibia are arid southern African states; Madagascar and Mozambique produce spices and other cash crops but not cocoa at any comparable scale.

items.value: Gomati – Ghaghara – Gandak – Kosi
items.reasoning: Going downstream (eastward) from Prayagraj, the Gomati joins the Ganga first, at Kaithi in Ghazipur district of Uttar Pradesh (about 83.5°E). The Ghaghara joins next, near Chhapra/Revelganj in Bihar (about 84.6°E), then the Gandak at Hajipur opposite Patna (about 85.2°E), and finally the Kosi near Kursela in Katihar district (about 87.2°E). The west-to-east sequence is therefore Gomati, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi.

items.value: Both Statement-II and Statement-III are correct and both explain why rainfall weathers rocks
items.reasoning: Rain water dissolves atmospheric carbon dioxide to form weak carbonic acid, which drives carbonation — the classic chemical weathering of limestone and other carbonate rocks — so Statement-II is correct and explains Statement-I. Rain water also carries dissolved atmospheric oxygen, and oxidation weathering (the rusting and crumbling of iron-bearing minerals) occurs precisely where oxygenated water reaches the rock, so Statement-III is correct and also explains Statement-I. Runner-up is B (only one of them explains): B would win if the setter regarded only carbonation as a genuinely rain-water-mediated weathering process and treated dissolved oxygen as incidental to the rainfall rather than a cause of weathering by it.

items.value: Only two — Germany and Norway border the North Sea; Finland and Russia do not
items.reasoning: The North Sea is enclosed by the United Kingdom, Norway, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and France. Germany's north-western coast and Norway's south-western coast both front it. Finland has no North Sea frontage at all — its coasts are on the Gulf of Bothnia and the Gulf of Finland, both arms of the Baltic. Russia's western sea outlets are the Baltic (Gulf of Finland and Kaliningrad) and, in the far north, the Barents Sea; neither is the North Sea.

items.value: Only one row (Hundru – Chota Nagpur – Subarnarekha) is correctly matched
items.reasoning: Row 2 is fully correct: Hundru Falls is on the Subarnarekha river near Ranchi, on the Chota Nagpur plateau. Row 3 is wrong on the river — Gersoppa (Jog) Falls is on the Sharavathi, not the Netravati, though it is indeed in the Western Ghats. Row 1 names the right river but the wrong region: the Dhuandhar falls are on the Narmada at Bhedaghat near Jabalpur, in the Narmada valley between the Vindhyas and the Satpuras, whereas the Malwa plateau lies north of the Vindhyas and is drained by the Chambal and Betwa. Runner-up is B (only two): B would win if the region column for row 1 were read loosely enough to let 'Malwa' stand for the wider Madhya Pradesh plateau country, since the river there is unquestionably correct.

items.value: Only two — the Appalachians and the Andes rows are correct; the Vosges and Alps rows are not
items.reasoning: Row 3 is correct: the Appalachians are old fold mountains in North America. Row 4 is correct: the Andes are young fold mountains in South America. Row 1 is wrong twice over — the Vosges are in Europe (eastern France), not Central Asia, and they are block mountains, a horst standing beside the Rhine rift valley opposite the Black Forest. Row 2 is wrong on type — the Alps are in Europe but are the textbook example of young fold mountains, not block mountains. The row-1 and row-2 errors look like a deliberate swap of the two mountain types.

items.value: Donyi Polo Airport and Kushinagar International Airport were built as greenfield projects; Vijayawada was not
items.reasoning: Donyi Polo Airport at Hollongi near Itanagar and Kushinagar International Airport in Uttar Pradesh both appear in the Ministry of Civil Aviation's list of greenfield airports approved in principle and were built on fresh sites. Vijayawada International Airport is the long-established Gannavaram aerodrome, which was expanded and given a new integrated terminal — a brownfield upgrade of an operating airport, not a greenfield project; Andhra Pradesh's greenfield airports are Bhogapuram, Dagadarthi and Oravakal. Runner-up is D (all three): D would win if the setter counted Vijayawada's new terminal and runway extension as a greenfield development in its own right.

items.value: Only statement 1 is correct — water vapour decreases with altitude, but its percentage is maximum in the warm humid tropics, not at the poles
items.reasoning: Water vapour is concentrated in the lowest layers of the atmosphere; roughly 90 per cent of it lies below about 5 km and it becomes negligible above the troposphere, so statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is the reverse of the truth: warm air holds far more moisture than cold air, so water vapour reaches up to about 4 per cent of the air by volume in the warm, wet tropics and falls below 1 per cent over the cold polar regions.

items.value: Marine West coast (cool temperate western margin) climate
items.reasoning: The decisive clue is the third description: annual precipitation between 50 cm and 250 cm distributed through the whole year is the standard figure for the marine west coast climate, where onshore westerlies and travelling depressions bring rain in every month, and the sea's moderating influence keeps both the annual and the daily temperature range small. The China type and humid subtropical climates (which are the same climate under two names) have a marked summer maximum of rainfall and a much larger annual temperature range. Runner-up is A (Equatorial): equatorial regions also have rain in all months and a famously tiny annual range, but their rainfall normally exceeds 200 cm rather than starting at 50 cm, and textbooks stress that the equatorial DAILY range is larger than the annual range rather than low. A would win if the setter weighted the low-range clue above the precipitation figure.

items.value: Both statements are correct — the Coriolis force rises with wind speed and is maximum at the poles, zero at the equator
items.reasoning: The Coriolis force is proportional to 2·m·v·Ω·sin(latitude). Because wind velocity v appears directly in that expression, the force increases as the wind blows faster, so statement 1 is correct. Because sin(latitude) is 1 at the poles and 0 at the equator, the force is maximum at the poles and absent at the equator, so statement 2 is correct too — which is why cyclones cannot form on the equator itself.

items.value: Only the Tropic of Cancer and the Arctic Circle get more than 12 hours of sunlight on June 21
items.reasoning: On 21 June the sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer and the northern hemisphere is tilted sunward, so every northern latitude has a day longer than 12 hours: the Tropic of Cancer gets roughly 13.5 hours and the Arctic Circle gets 24 hours of continuous daylight. The equator is the one latitude with almost exactly 12 hours of day and night throughout the year, so it does not exceed 12 hours. The Tropic of Capricorn is in its winter and receives only about 10.5 hours.

items.value: The Congo Basin
items.reasoning: The Cuvette Centrale peatlands of the central Congo Basin, straddling the Republic of the Congo and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, were mapped in 2017 as the world's largest tropical peatland complex, storing on the order of 30 billion tonnes of carbon — roughly three years of global fossil-fuel emissions. Draining or burning them would release that store, which is why oil exploration and logging licences there attract international concern. Amazonian and New Guinean (Kikori) peatlands are far smaller, and the Rio de la Plata basin is grassland and cropland rather than peat.

items.value: All three statements about PFAS are correct
items.reasoning: PFAS have been detected worldwide in drinking water, in food and in grease-resistant food packaging such as wrappers and moulded fibre containers, so statement 1 is correct. Their carbon–fluorine bonds are among the strongest in organic chemistry, which is why they resist degradation and are nicknamed 'forever chemicals' — statement 2 is correct. That persistence, combined with their binding to blood proteins, causes them to build up in the tissues of animals and humans over repeated exposure, so statement 3 is correct as well.

items.value: Only three of the five groups — carabid beetles, flies and wasps — contain parasitoid species
items.reasoning: Parasitoids (organisms whose larvae develop on or in a single host and eventually kill it) are concentrated in the Hymenoptera, where parasitoid wasps are the archetype, and in the Diptera, where the family Tachinidae is entirely parasitoid. Among beetles, the Carabidae include genuine parasitoid lineages such as Brachinus and many Lebiinae, whose larvae develop on the pupae of other beetles. Centipedes are free-living predators that kill and consume many prey rather than developing on one host, and termites are social detritivores and wood-feeders with no parasitoid members. Runner-up is A (only two): A would win if the setter treated Carabidae as strictly predatory and counted only flies and wasps, though the deliberate naming of 'carabid' rather than simply 'beetles' suggests the parasitoid carabids are the point of the item.

items.value: All three — groundnut, horse-gram and soybean all belong to the pea family (Fabaceae)
items.reasoning: Groundnut (Arachis hypogaea), horse-gram (Macrotyloma uniflorum) and soybean (Glycine max) are all legumes in the family Fabaceae, the pea or bean family, and all three bear the family's characteristic pod fruit and root nodules housing nitrogen-fixing rhizobia. Groundnut is sometimes mistaken for a nut because of its name and its oilseed use, but botanically it is a legume whose pods ripen underground.

items.value: Statement-I is correct (fruit bats are listed as vermin), but Statement-II is wrong — the Indian Flying Fox eats fruit, not blood
items.reasoning: The Indian Flying Fox is a large fruit bat, and fruit bats were listed in Schedule V, the vermin schedule, of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 alongside the common crow, rats and mice — so Statement-I stands as printed. Statement-II is plainly false: the Indian Flying Fox is a frugivore and nectar feeder and an important pollinator and seed disperser. Blood-feeding is confined to the three vampire bat species of Central and South America, which do not occur in India. Since Statement-II is false, options A, B and D are all excluded.

items.value: Insects
items.reasoning: All three are insects of the order Hemiptera, the true bugs. Cicadas and froghoppers (spittlebugs, whose nymphs hide in frothy 'cuckoo spit') belong to the sap-sucking Auchenorrhyncha, and the pond skater or water strider is a gerrid bug that walks on the surface film of still water. None is a bird, fish or reptile.

items.value: Both statements are correct and the plastic gum base explains why discarded chewing gum pollutes
items.reasoning: Most commercial chewing gums no longer use natural chicle; their gum base is built from synthetic polymers such as polyisobutylene, polyvinyl acetate and styrene-butadiene rubber, which are plastics — so Statement-II is correct. Because that base is a non-biodegradable plastic, spat-out gum persists on pavements and in soil and water and breaks down only into microplastics, which is exactly why chewing gum is treated as a source of environmental pollution. Statement-II is therefore not merely a companion fact but the reason for Statement-I.

items.value: None of the three pairs is correctly matched
items.reasoning: The indri is the largest living lemur and, like all lemurs, is endemic to Madagascar, not Brazil. The bonobo is endemic to the forests south of the Congo river in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, not Madagascar — so rows 1 and 3 have in effect had their countries exchanged. Elk are deer of the cool northern forests of North America and Eurasia and do not occur in tropical Indonesia. All three pairs are therefore wrong.

items.value: Only statement 2 is correct — the World Toilet Organization is an NGO, not a UN agency, and it does not disburse funds
items.reasoning: The World Toilet Organization is a non-profit body founded in Singapore in 2001 by Jack Sim; it is not an organ or specialised agency of the United Nations, so statement 1 is wrong. Statement 2 is correct: the World Toilet Summit, World Toilet Day and the World Toilet College are all its initiatives, and World Toilet Day was later adopted by the UN General Assembly as an official observance in 2013. Statement 3 is wrong because the organization works through advocacy, awareness and training rather than by granting funds to countries.

items.value: Statements 1 and 2 are correct; male leopards do scent-mark their territory, so statement 3 is wrong
items.reasoning: Lions are non-seasonal breeders and mate at any time of year, so statement 1 is correct. Cheetahs lack the specialised loose hyoid and laryngeal structure that lets Panthera species roar; they chirp, purr and yowl instead, so statement 2 is correct. Statement 3 is false: male leopards are strongly territorial and advertise their range exactly as male lions do, by spraying urine on trees and bushes, making scrapes and rubbing scent from facial glands, in addition to rasping calls.
